title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6811 – Reuters estimate
body: Yesterday the PNoC made moves to slow the yuan appreciation: China's PBOC lifts FX reserve ratio to 6%: what it means for the yuan, AUD --- The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

title: WP - 2026-11-04 - Simon Beyeler: Forecasting the post-COVID inflation surge in Switzerland
body: The surge in inflation after the COVID-19 pandemic caught forecasters and policy makers by surprise: shocks treated as transitory turned out to be persistent, producing large forecast errors. Watson (2026) asks whether the U.S. surge could instead have been recognised as persistent in real time using Unobserved-Components Stochastic Volatility (UC-SV) models. This paper replicates and extends that exercise for Switzerland, using (i) total Swiss CPI inflation and (ii) sectoral inflation for 22 expenditure groups - both extended with an explicit seasonal component since the Swiss CPI is not seasonally adjusted. Both models attribute the bulk of the 2021-2023 Swiss surge to the permanent trend rather than to transitory noise and reach that reading from data available in real time. In the sectoral model, the sector-specific trends account for most of the variance, whereas the common inflation trend plays only a minor role.

For background, the Institute for Supply Management's Services PMI is one of the most closely watched monthly gauges of the US economy. It's released at 10 am ET on the third business day of the month, two days after its manufacturing counterpart, and is based on a survey of purchasing and supply executives at services firms. The report was known as the non-manufacturing index until 2020. Like other PMIs, it's a diffusion index where readings above 50 signal expansion and below 50 signal contraction. The headline is a composite of four equally weighted sub-indexes: business activity, new orders, employment and supplier deliveries. Because services make up the bulk of US economic activity and employment, the survey is often seen as a better reflection of the broader economy than the manufacturing ISM. The prices index is frequently the most market-moving part of the report. It measures the share of firms paying higher prices for inputs and has become a key early signal for services inflation, which the Federal Reserve watches closely.

title: The biggest loser of the US elections was data centers
body: One of the clearest messages from Tuesday's US midterm elections had nothing to do with Republicans or Democrats. It was a resounding rejection of data centers. Communities across the country voted on dozens of ballot measures involving data-center construction, zoning, moratoriums and development restrictions. Almost everywhere, voters came down on the same side: against new development. The margins were extraordinary in many places. Granville, Ohio: 82.5% voted to prohibit data centers. Sunbury, Ohio: 78.6% supported a ban on large data centers, potentially affecting a proposed $2 billion Amazon project. Trenton, Ohio: 79.6% backed restrictions on large-scale data centers. Edgewater, Florida: 77.6% supported a ban on new data centers and expansions. Bloomington, Illinois: 77.6% supported an advisory moratorium. Alhambra, California: 82.4% supported a ban, with counting still incomplete. Boulder City, Nevada: 70.6% opposed allowing data centers in a designated development area. Ashville, Ohio: 81.6% rejected a development agreement involving EdgeConneX. Downe Township, New Jersey: 87.3% opposed data-center development in an advisory vote. In Illinois, four Madison County townships voted on whether officials should permit data centers. All four rejected the idea, with opposition ranging from roughly 74% to 83%. title: Morning Kickstart: Dollar falls, stocks rise as Democrats take Congress

Democrats have won control of both the House and Senate, setting up divided government for the final two years of President Trump's term. The new Congress takes office in January. For traders, the immediate question is how much of the initial reaction can hold. Lower yields and falling oil provide a more supportive backdrop for equity buyers, but the election result alone does not determine the next trend. Inflation, employment, earnings and the Fed remain key barometers. A tougher legislative path in Washington The result gives Democrats greater power to challenge the administration through congressional investigations, negotiations over legislation and Senate approval of presidential nominees. Trump retains his veto, leaving both sides facing limits on what they can deliver. From a market perspective, additional tax cuts and major spending packages could face higher hurdles. That could temper expectations for further fiscal stimulus and help explain the focus on lower Treasury yields. However, divided government also creates the potential for confrontations over government funding and the debt ceiling. Technology oversight is another area to watch, including artificial intelligence, data centers and cryptocurrencies. Greater scrutiny would not automatically translate into sweeping legislation.

title: How Congressional control shapes US fiscal policy and financial markets
body: US elections can have a significant impact on financial markets, not only because they determine who controls the government but also because they influence expectations about future fiscal policy. One of the most important aspects of the US political system is that Congress controls the government's spending and taxation decisions, giving election outcomes the potential to reshape the economic outlook. When one party controls both chambers of Congress, passing legislation can become easier. Conversely, divided government, where different parties control the presidency, the House and/or the Senate, can create political gridlock and make major fiscal changes more difficult. These political dynamics matter because fiscal policy influences economic growth, inflation, government borrowing and, ultimately, the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook. How congress controls fiscal policy The US Congress plays a central role in determining fiscal policy through three main channels: government spending, taxation and borrowing. It approves federal spending through appropriations legislation, determining how much money is allocated to areas such as defence, infrastructure, healthcare and social programmes. The President can propose a budget, but Congress ultimately decides what spending legislation to pass. Congress also determines federal tax policy.

title: How will central banks wrap up the year?
body: The Fed, the ECB, and the Bank of Japan all kept rates on hold last week, just as expected. December is unlikely to bring any surprises either: unless the Middle East crisis eases, the base case is a rate hike, except perhaps in Japan, where the huge debt burden leaves little room for tightening. But why not act now? Starting with the Fed, the case for a hike is already pretty compelling: inflation remains stubbornly high, hitting 3.6% year on year in September, while US growth is strong (GDP expanded at a 3.4% annualized rate in Q3 2026, up from 2.2% in Q2) and consumer spending and investment remain resilient. Hence, two FOMC members voted for a 25-basis-point hike. The rest of the committee, however, are holding back, apparently wary of what comes next in the Middle East: whether peace talks gain traction or tensions flare up again. Oil prices remain a key variable here: any renewed disruption to supply routes or energy infrastructure could push crude higher, adding to inflationary pressures and making a rate hike harder to avoid. And even though Washington has signed off on a draft deal with Iran, covering mutual concessions on its nuclear program and frozen assets, there's still no clear breakthrough in sight. As for the ECB, unlike in the US, consumption remains weak, there's no AI investment boom, and inflation is largely driven by energy costs, so it too chose to wait and see how the situation in the Middle East unfolds.

title: NZDUSD buyers defend the floor. Can they break the ceiling?
body: The NZDUSD moved lower after weaker New Zealand jobs data early in the new trading day, but sellers could not push the price below a familiar floor near 0.5579 (see green circles on the chart below). That level has attracted buyers on a number of occasions going back to late September and through October. Today, buyers leaned against it again and were rewarded with a rebound as the market reacted to the US election results. The hold matters technically. Buyers had a level to define and limit risk, and they defended it. However, holding support is only the first step. To increase the bullish bias, they now need to take back resistance above. The 200-hour moving average stalled the rebound The rally today off the solid floor, broke above its 100 hour moving average near 0.5622, but ran into the falling 200-hour moving average (green line) near 0.56418. Sellers leaned against that level and stalled the move higher, keeping that moving average as a key topside barometer. Get above—and stay above—and buyers would give themselves more control. Until then, sellers can point to the failed test as evidence that overhead resistance is still doing its job. Ahead of that level, the 100-hour moving average near 0.5622 and the swing area from 0.56256 to 0.56333 provide nearer hurdles. Buyers need to establish support above those levels to put the 200-hour moving average back in their sights. What comes next?

title: The market is making a big bet on ending the Iran war
body: If endless Middle East wars were on the ballot, it's safe to say how it would have gone. Republicans are openly blaming the war for the midterm rout and the market is taking that at face value. The indication is that Trump will be forced out of Iran, and possibly soon. That will mean a reopened Hormuz and oil will be flowing again. The market is aggressively pricing it in with WTI down $7.69 to $88.39 today in one of the largest plunges of the war. The close was the lowest since August 31. Given the oil hit $105 late last week, that's a huge turn. It's a big drag for inflation too and you can see that in the Treasury market with yields down 3-6 basis points, though there are certainly puts and takes there with Democrats now looking like they're destined to hold the Senate for the next 4-6 years. I fear that a deal to end the war may prove difficult. Trump has been trying to extract the US from it for months with little success and I wonder how eager Iran will be to deal after the vote. If a deal is made, I also wonder how fast the oil can move and how quickly inventories can be rebuilt. Refineries are already running full-tilt and inventories have been drawn down heavily. Looking out the oil and gasoline futures curves, today's drops have been consistent so there is some real optimism there, but so many times during this war, that optimism has proven misplaced. There are leaks today about positive developments and there seems to be a deal on the table.

title: Gold is taking it clue from the USD and yields moving lower. Technicals are also giving the buyers a push.
body: Gold is trading up more than $130, or 3.3%, at $4061.80. The price reached a high of $4070.53 after trading as low as $3919.93. Lower Treasury yields and a weaker US dollar are helping fuel the gains. The US 10-year yield is down 6.6 basis points at 4.883%, near its lowest level since September 10. Why do lower yields and a weaker USD support gold? A weaker USD makes gold less expensive for overseas buyers. Gold is priced internationally in dollars. When the dollar falls against currencies like the euro or yen, buyers using those currencies can purchase the same ounce for less, assuming the dollar gold price is unchanged. That can encourage demand. Lower yields reduce the opportunity cost of holding gold. Gold pays no interest. When Treasury yields fall, investors give up less interest income by owning gold instead of bonds, making the precious metal relatively more attractive. Technical support provided the foundation Recall that Monday's low tested the rising 100-week moving average and a lower channel trendline near $3870. Buyers leaned against that support and pushed the price higher, establishing a base for today's advance. Today, buyers strengthened their control by pushing above the 100-hour moving average at $3960 and the 200-hour moving average at $3993.19. Those breaks shifted the shorter-term bias higher and helped accelerate the move toward $4070.53. The support held. Resistance broke. Buyers gained more control.

title: The market is telling the hyperscalers it's happy about a slower data center buildout
body: Perhaps the clearest takeaway from Tuesday's US midterms is that data centers are unpopular. After a short-lived construction boom, they provide little ongoing employment and drive up local energy costs. There were 41 local votes on data center curbs and 40 of them are on track to win, with margins in the 75/25% range. Microsoft and Amazon are heavily into the data center business, including huge plans to build more so they should be losers today, right? Wrong. Shares of those two are up around 7% and the market cheers a slower, smaller data center buildout. The market has been hating the massive spending on highly-inflated chips and data center supply chains. In effect, the market is saying that the government is doing for you what you should be doing. Now the companies themselves have been trying to sell Wall Street on data center economics but the cash demands are simply too high and the market has said that the risk-reward isn't convincing. At this point, there might be some reflexivity in company management. Now that they've seen how the stock reacts to data center curbs, they might slow their own ambitions to levels closer to matching free cash flow. If so, that could be a powerful tailwind for the stocks, which have struggled this year. Amazon is particularly compelling as its core business of goods delivery isn't under threat from AI in the same way as a software company like Microsoft.

body: It's largely true election loss was the result of the Iran war It was worth it You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon I'll get along probably with Democrats If I were on the ballot we would have won We weren't able to transfer the love to candidates It would destroy Democratic Part if they impeach me Notably, JD Vance wrote at length about the election loss and also blamed the Iran war. Vance: One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us." Well, that looks prophetic now.

title: House Democratic leader Jeffries says will pass bill to stop tariffs and to end the Iran War
body: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries says Democrats will pursue legislation to stop President Trump's tariffs and bring an end to the war with Iran. He also wants to reverse Medicaid cuts and restore the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits, placing healthcare costs at the center of his affordability agenda. The proposals target four areas: Tariffs: Reassert congressional authority over trade policy and seek to roll back Trump's tariffs. Jeffries argues that those duties have increased the cost of everyday goods. Iran: Pursue legislation to end U.S. involvement in the war. He has said Democrats should examine available legislative options, including Congress's control over funding, without committing to a specific funding restriction. Medicaid: Reverse cuts enacted under the Republican tax and spending law, seeking to preserve coverage and access to care. ACA tax credits: Restore enhanced premium assistance to reduce out-of-pocket insurance costs for people buying coverage through the ACA marketplaces. For markets, the potential implications run through import costs, energy prices and healthcare funding. Tariff relief could ease costs for importers, while progress toward ending the war could reduce oil's geopolitical risk premium. Restoring healthcare support could benefit hospitals and insurers exposed to Medicaid and ACA coverage. Those are potential effects, dependent on the details and whether the proposals become law.
